## Key claims (as stated in source)
- Data-centre water is rarely viewed as a constraint, but if data-centre water consumption is not dramatically reduced it will be an increasingly important factor in data-centre location.
- AI expansion is linked to data-centre growth; rising demand for compute (inference/training, deep learning) requires GPUs/TPUs hosted in data centres.
- Investment context: **Goldman Sachs** estimates leading tech giants, other companies, and utilities will spend **~$1tn on capex in coming years** (data centres, chips, AI infrastructure, power grid). **IDC** projects **global AI spending to reach $632 billion by 2028**.
- Some forecasts predict a **doubling of US data-centre power consumption to 35 GW by end of decade**, almost double its 2022 level.
- Water measured by **withdrawal** (taken and returned) vs **consumption** (lost, usually evaporation). US average water intensity for electricity generation was **2.18 litres per kWh in 2015**; moving to wind/solar could reduce US water withdrawals by **25%**.
- Cooling: water circulated through pipes/cooling towers (evaporative cooling); redundant cooling systems need reliable water. **Less than one-third of data-centre operators tracked any water metrics**, and water conservation ranked low priority; Google called out for treating water use as a trade secret.
- Alternatives: direct/indirect air cooling, refrigerants, **immersion cooling** (dielectric fluids), geothermal cooling, phase-change materials.
- **Global data centres:** US hosts the largest number, **39% of the total — 2,928 data centres in the US** (3,168 in North America) of **7,597 globally**; Western Europe 1,888; Asia 788.
- **Water-stress table (WRI Aqueduct baseline):** USA 2,928 DCs, score 2.6 (Medium–High) current / 2.8 (2050 BAU); China 106 DCs, 2.8 (Medium–High); India 236 DCs, 4.1 (Extremely High); Italy 138, 3.3 (High); Turkey 81, 3.4 (High); etc.
